entries.label: Thinks an event happens only when the outcome is the whole event set
entries.description: The student treats an event like {2, 4, 6} as a single outcome that must come up as a whole, instead of seeing that the event occurs when the outcome is any one element of the set.

refutation.text_md: You are treating the event as one big outcome, so you think it only happens if the whole set turns up. It is natural to read $A = \{2, 4, 6\}$ as a single item, but it is a collection of outcomes.
A dice shows only one number per roll. If the whole set had to appear, the event 'getting an even number' could never happen, because one roll never shows 2, 4 and 6 together.

The book's rule is that an event occurred if the outcome of the experiment is an element of the set that expresses the event. If the dice shows 4, then 4 is in $\{2, 4, 6\}$, so the even-number event occurred.
This is also why we count elements: $P(A) = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)} = \frac{3}{6}$ counts the 3 outcomes that each make $A$ occur, out of the 6 possible outcomes.
Next time, ask 'Is the outcome one of the elements of the event set?' If yes, the event occurred. Then count those elements for $n(A)$.

verdict.reason: The book's caution says an event occurred if the outcome is an element of the event set. The error of treating the event as one outcome that must appear as a whole is a plausible reading of that caution. The refutation is mathematically correct: one roll shows one number, and a roll of 4 is in {2,4,6}. P(A)=3/6 matches the canonical n(A)/n(S). It cites no question ids, pages or figures, and it teaches nothing beyond the book.

dropped.label: Mixes up 'mutually exclusive' with 'having an overlap'
dropped.reason: The maths is right: B∩C=φ, P=0/8=0, and A={2,4,6}, B={1,3,5} give 0/6=0. But step 2 tells the student to 'Take B and C in the Venn diagram example', which is a figure the student cannot see. The entry also blurs two different errors: thinking mutually exclusive means overlapping, and saying 'not possible to find' instead of 0. Step 1 invents a diagnosis ('a name for events in the same sample space') that the evidence does not support. The book only says B and C cannot occur at the same time. It has no signal, so none can misdiagnose a student.

entries.label: Adds P(A) and P(B) and forgets the overlap
entries.description: The student finds P(A ∪ B) by adding P(A) and P(B) even though the events share outcomes, so shared outcomes are counted twice.
entries.signal: A probability for A ∪ B that is exactly P(A) + P(B), larger than the true value, when A and B overlap (e.g. 7/10 instead of 3/5, or 7/9 instead of 2/3).

refutation.text_md: You are thinking "A or B means add the two probabilities". That is right when A and B have nothing in common, and it is a good start. The trouble starts when they share an outcome.
Take cards numbered 1 to 9. $A$ is an even number, $A=\{2,4,6,8\}$, so $P(A)=\frac{4}{9}$. $B$ is a number divisible by 3, $B=\{3,6,9\}$, so $P(B)=\frac{3}{9}$. Adding gives $\frac{7}{9}$.
Now list $A\cup B$ itself: $\{2,3,4,6,8,9\}$. That is only 6 cards, so $P(A\cup B)=\frac{6}{9}=\frac{2}{3}$, not $\frac{7}{9}$. The card 6 is in both $A$ and $B$, so adding counted it twice.
Take the shared outcomes away once: $A\cap B=\{6\}$, so $P(A\cap B)=\frac{1}{9}$, and $\frac{4}{9}+\frac{3}{9}-\frac{1}{9}=\frac{6}{9}=\frac{2}{3}$, which matches.
Next time, first find $A\cap B$. If it has outcomes in it, use $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$. If $A\cap B$ is empty (mutually exclusive), the subtraction is $0$ and you just add.

verdict.reason: The error is real. Adding P(A) and P(B) gives 7/10 instead of 3/5 in drill (a), and 7/9 instead of 2/3 in the cards example. The refutation uses the book's own cards 1–9 example. Its numbers match the canonical solution: A={2,4,6,8}, B={3,6,9}, A∪B has 6 cards, P=2/3, and 4/9+3/9−1/9=2/3. It shows the double-count by listing A∪B directly, then applies the book's formula and the mutually exclusive case. It cites no question ids, pages or figures, and no review history.

flags.text: The only evidence is the remark P(A) + P(A') = P(S) = 1. It states the rule and names no error. There are no book caution boxes, no wrong options and no widget predicates for this objective, so I wrote no entries. Any entry would rest on my own guesses about common errors, not on evidence.
The remark prints the complement as A` (backtick), and the canonical solutions use A'. I kept the book's wording and wrote nothing student-facing.

entries.label: Counts the whole set A when asked for A only
entries.description: The student takes the 'only' event A - B to be the whole set A, so they use all of A's students and never remove the overlap A ∩ B.
entries.signal: Gives 18/40 (or 9/20) for reading Al-Akhbar only, or 15/40 (or 3/8) for Al-Ahram only.

refutation.text_md: You are treating 'reads Al-Akhbar' and 'reads Al-Akhbar only' as the same event. You were right to start from the 18 students in set A.

Those 18 students are made of two groups. Some read only Al-Akhbar. Others read Al-Akhbar and Al-Ahram too, and that second group is the 8 in $A \cap B$. This is what $(A - B) \cup (A \cap B) = A$ says.
The 8 students who read both also read Al-Ahram, so they do not belong to 'Al-Akhbar only'. Answering $\frac{18}{40}$ counts them as well.
Take the overlap away: $n(A - B) = 18 - 8 = 10$, so $P(A - B) = \frac{10}{40} = \frac{1}{4}$, not $\frac{18}{40}$.
Whenever a question says 'only', subtract the overlap first: $n(A - B) = n(A) - n(A \cap B)$. Then divide by $n(S)$.

verdict.reason: The figure shows B-only 7, overlap 8, A-only 10 and outside 15, with n(S)=40. The refutation's numbers (18, 8, 10, 10/40 = 1/4) match the canonical solution. It uses the book's identity (A-B)∪(A∩B)=A. It targets the error of counting all of A, and it cites no question ids, pages or review history. The 15/40 form of the signal also equals the outside-region count, but the 18/40 case is clear and the signal is acceptable.
